1.pericope_label: How amiable are thy tabernacles: the longing for the courts and the birds that nest at the altars

schools.summary: Augustine works from a title reading for the winepresses and, finding no press mentioned in the psalm, takes the pressing spiritually of those conformed to the image of the Son, who was himself first pressed in his Passion.

Calvin traces the sons named in the title to the rebel whose children were spared and became porters and singers, argues for David as author against the notion that the Levites wrote it for him, and allows one difficulty in the mention of the hill; Gill reports that the word for the bird means any bird and that the versions differ.

Henry would rather live in a bird nest near the altars than in a palace at a distance from them, and explains the plural by the courts; Spurgeon says the psalmist does not tell us how lovely the dwellings were because he could not, and loved the sanctuary in every part.

Clarke judges it very unlikely that birds were allowed to nest about altars of such purity and offers three ways of construing the clause, and gives the descent and offices of the sons named in the title; Wesley takes those who dwell in the house as the priests and Levites and the devout who were there perpetually.

Ellicott denies that the verse presents any real difficulty and supports birds about a temple from ancient and modern parallels, rules out the comparison on grounds of Hebrew style, treats the plurals as merely poetic, and derives the verb of longing from a root meaning to grow pale; Keil and Delitzsch place the psalm at the head of the second half of a collection and defend its stylistic character against a critic.

debates: Could birds have nested at the altars? Clarke thinks it very unlikely, given the purity required and the perpetual fires, and offers to read the clause as a parenthesis, to transpose it, or to take the whole as a comparison; Ellicott answers that there is no real occasion for the difficulty, that nesting on the altars themselves would be absurd but nesting in and about the temple quite probable, cites three parallels ancient and modern, and rules out the comparison Clarke prefers on the ground that Hebrew style is not favourable to simile.

Why do the nouns stand in the plural? Gill, Henry, Clarke and Spurgeon all explain it by the divisions of the sanctuary, the holy place, the holy of holies and the courts where the people stood; Ellicott answers that the plural is used poetically and that we need not think of the courts at all.
outliers: Augustine expounds a title reading for the winepresses, observing that the psalm mentions no press or vat, and takes the grape and olive hanging in free air until they are pressed as a figure of those conformed to the image of the Son.

Ellicott supports the presence of birds about a temple from an old historian who tells of nests of young sparrows taken at a Greek shrine, from a story of a man slain for harming a sparrow that sheltered in another, and from a traveller report of birds nesting in the sanctuary at Mecca.
themes: birds settled where the worshipper cannot be
the blessedness of those who dwell there

5.pericope_label: Blessed is the man whose strength is in thee: the pilgrim road, the valley of Baca, and the going from strength to strength

schools.summary: Spurgeon corrects the clause about the ways to thy ways and calls that far better, and finds the pilgrims refreshed even in the dreariest part of the road; Henry takes the face of the anointed of the Mediator rather than of the psalmist.

Gill collects the older identifications of the valley and declines to fix on any, keeps the pits and the rain, and multiplies senses for the going from strength to strength, from company to company and from class to class in the school of Christ.

Clarke declares the received clause about the ways no sense and reads the highways of the temple, identifies the valley with the place of weeping on the authority of seven manuscripts, turns the second half of that verse into a promise about teachers clothed with blessings, and calls the close of the next verse a bad paraphrase and no translation; Wesley keeps the dug pits and the rain that fills them.

Ellicott derives the highways from a root meaning to cast up and subordinates the moral sense to the pilgrimage, weighs four identifications of the valley and prefers the sterile one, reads blessings rather than pools with the received text, and reports an emendation of the following verse; Keil and Delitzsch make the divine strength mighty in the man weakness.

debates: What stands in the second half of the sixth verse? Ellicott holds that rain is the right rendering of the first word and that where our version gives pools the text itself gives blessings, a reading now generally adopted, so that the autumn rain covers the valley with blessings; Clarke reads the same consonants quite differently, as saying that the instructor is clothed with blessings, so that God gives teachers after his own heart who are watered while they water the people; Gill and Wesley keep the pits dug for relief and the rain that fills them.

How does the seventh verse end? Clarke calls the received words a paraphrase, and a bad one, but no translation, and renders that the God of gods shall be seen in Zion; Ellicott agrees that the expression is hardly Hebrew in either sense and that the text is suspicious, reporting an emendation that makes the pilgrims go to the temple of the living God to see the God of gods there; Gill instead multiplies senses for the earlier phrase.
outliers: Clarke turns the disputed clause into a promise about ministers, reading that the instructor is covered with blessings, so that those who water the people are themselves watered while they do it.

Ellicott weighs four identifications of the valley, a valley of trouble, the valley of the giants, one found near the mount of the law by a traveller, and one identified more recently on the caravan route from the north, and prefers the second because it is elsewhere described as sterile.
themes: the pilgrim road kept in the heart
a dry valley turned into a spring
a text suspected at two points

9.pericope_label: Behold, O God our shield: the day in the courts, the threshold of the house, and the sun and shield

schools.summary: Spurgeon reads the prayer both as a nation prayer for its king and a believer prayer for the Son of David, and holds the lowest station in the house better than the highest outside it, since only to wait at the threshold and peep within is bliss.

Gill reports two Jewish readings of the shield and prefers to apply the whole to Christ, takes the one day of the sabbath and now of the day of public worship, and divides the sun and shield between light and defence.

Clarke applies the anointed to the Mediator while listing the other applications and allowing each its reasons, turns the preference for the threshold into a question for the reader conscience, and defends the reading sun against an emendation on the authority of a prophet and of the manuscripts; Wesley makes the psalmist himself the anointed and divides the two figures plainly.

Ellicott puts shield and anointed in direct parallelism, and would render the next clause as waiting on the threshold as one unworthy to enter, granting that the notion of a doorkeeper suits a psalm of the family who kept the gates.

debates: Who is the anointed whose face God is asked to regard? Wesley takes it of the psalmist himself, a vile sinner yet an anointed king; Ellicott sets shield and anointed in direct parallelism, so that the king is the shield; Gill reports a reading that makes the shield the sanctuary and a better one that makes it the king, and prefers to apply the whole to Christ; Clarke reads it of the Mediator while granting that others apply it to the psalmist, to the leader of the return and to the people, each with his reasons; Spurgeon keeps the national and the christological sense together.

Is doorkeeper the right rendering? Ellicott would render instead that he had rather wait on the threshold as one not worthy to enter, the old versions making it a being rejected in scorn, and grants only that the notion of a doorkeeper suits a psalm of the family who kept the gates of the tabernacle; Spurgeon and Clarke keep the office, Spurgeon holding the lowest station in the house better than the highest outside.
outliers: Clarke defends the rendering sun against a scholar who would read guardian instead, on the ground that representing God as the sun is without example in Scripture, answering with the prophet promise that the Sun of righteousness should arise with healing in his wings and noting that no manuscript supports the change.
Ellicott sets beside the preference for the threshold the words a Greek dramatist gives the boy who sweeps the threshold of a temple, calling it a pleasant task and an honoured one.
themes: a king held up before God
one day weighed against a thousand
the threshold preferred to the tent
light and defence in one name
